summary:
Jigawa State's own criminal layer is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). It operates alongside the national framework rather than replacing it: the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) treats the Sharia penal layer as the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa. A trans visitor who is Muslim by the state's reckoning is therefore exposed to the state code's offences and penalties, not only to the national statute.

The Home Office's Sharia penalties table covering twelve northern states records Jigawa's penalties under the Sharia Penal Code (2000): married men face death by stoning; unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The sourcebook on Sharia implementation in northern Nigeria records the same structure and places Jigawa among four states whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm), with lesbianism carrying up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment. Exposure turns on the sex and marital status a Sharia court applies to the person before it. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship sits in the women's tier where that is how the court reads the conduct, and in the heavier tier where the conduct is classified as sodomy between men, reaching rajm where the court treats the person as a married man.

The Jigawa code reaches conduct the national statute does not cover, including same-sex conduct between women, and its own explanation of the offence includes the "unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs".

Jigawa is among twelve northern states that had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, and those states remain the only ones where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, as recorded by Human Rights Watch in 2004.
tangentialFactors:
Jigawa's sodomy penalty structure is shared with three other northern states. The Home Office note's discussion of Sharia law (section 8.2.20) is organised around the codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other northern states, with Jigawa's penalties taken from the same twelve-state table rather than a Jigawa-specific section.

The state code and the national statute run in parallel, so conduct may fall under the Jigawa offence even where it does not fall under the national prohibition, as with same-sex conduct between women.
localsOnly:
The Sharia penal layer applies to Muslims in Jigawa, so religious affiliation determines which criminal code governs a resident. Sharia courts in the state hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, and Jigawa is one of twelve northern states that adopted Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, the group that remains the only states where Sharia courts try criminal cases.

The Jigawa code criminalises same-sex conduct between women, which the national statute does not reach, so residents whose conduct falls outside the national prohibition remain within the state offence.

Residents convicted under the code face the tiers recorded in the sources: stoning to death for a married man, 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment for an unmarried man, and up to 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment for same-sex acts between women.
outOfScopeNotes:
No arrest, prosecution, charge or sentence under Jigawa's Sharia Penal Code was identified in the sources consulted. The enforcement record documented elsewhere in the country concerns other states, and no equivalent Jigawa case is sourced here.

Whether the stoning penalty for a married man has been imposed or carried out in Jigawa is not sourced, and no Jigawa Sharia court judgment interpreting the code's "unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs" wording was identified.

Whether Jigawa operates a morality enforcement body, and how any such body treats gender-nonconforming people, is not sourced.

Jigawa's penalties are drawn from a table covering twelve states and from the text of the code; the Home Office note's dedicated discussion of Sharia law is organised around other northern states' codes rather than a Jigawa-specific section.
